items.title: Trend of Niño 3.4 (OISST): rising

kpis.name: trend, 90 days
kpis.plain: Over the last 90 days the anomaly moved +0.46 °C per month on average; 95 % interval +0.42 … +0.51.

kpis.name: trend, 30 days
kpis.plain: The last month alone: +0.12 °C per month, slower than the 90-day pace.

kpis.name: probability of rising
kpis.plain: With a flat prior, the chance that the true 90-day slope is positive is 100 % (p = 0.000 two-sided).

kpis.name: acceleration
kpis.plain: Positive: the rise is speeding up; negative: it is slowing or turning.

method.name: Linear regression with a robust (Newey–West) error
method.plain: We draw the straight line that fits the last 90 days best and ask how sure we are of its slope. Daily values are not independent (warm days come in runs), so the ordinary error would be too optimistic; the Newey–West correction widens it honestly. The “probability of rising” is the Bayesian reading of the same numbers with no prior opinion.
method.tech: OLS on daily anomalies to 1991–2020, n = 90 and 30; HAC standard error with Bartlett weights, lag 7; two-sided p from the normal approximation; P(slope > 0) = Φ(t) under a flat prior. Residual sd 0.08 °C. Acceleration = slope(last 30) − slope(days −90…−30).
caveats: a 30-day slope is noisy: read it with its interval, not alone
a trend says where the series went, not where it will go; the analogue forecast is a separate method

items.title: Regime shift in Niño 3.4 (OISST): 2026-04-18, +2.08 °C (significant)

kpis.name: most likely break
kpis.plain: The day that best splits the last 400 days into “before” and “after”: mean -0.37 °C before, +1.72 °C after.

kpis.name: shift of the mean
kpis.plain: How much the average level jumped at the break.

kpis.name: chance it is noise
kpis.plain: Out of 300 random series with the same memory and spread, 4 produced a break at least this sharp. Small means the shift is real.

method.name: Change-point by binary segmentation, tested against red noise
method.plain: We try every day as a possible turning point and pick the one where the average before and after differ most. Then we ask whether a series with no real turn, only memory and noise, could show a jump this big by chance; if it rarely can, the shift is real.
method.tech: Single mean-shift change-point: max over t of |m₁−m₂|·√(t(n−t)/n)/sd, n = 400. Null: AR(1) with fitted φ = 0.99 and matched variance, 300 simulations, p = share with a larger statistic. Multiple breaks are not modelled.
caveats: one break only: a series with several turns shows the biggest
the break date is uncertain by days to weeks

items.title: Inertia of Niño 3.4 (OISST): memory 99 days, persistence says +2.31 °C in two weeks

kpis.name: memory of the series
kpis.plain: Day-to-day persistence φ = 0.99: a departure fades to a third in about 99 days if nothing pushes it.

kpis.name: persistence forecast, +14 d
kpis.plain: If the series only had its memory, in two weeks it would sit at +2.31 °C (80 % band ±0.17).

kpis.name: persistence forecast, +30 d
kpis.plain: In a month: +1.96 °C (80 % band ±0.23).

method.name: AR(1) persistence model
method.plain: The simplest forecast is “tomorrow looks like today, a little less so each day”. We measure how strongly each day follows the previous one and let that memory fade forward. It is the baseline any real forecast must beat; the analogue forecast on the panel is the other reading.
method.tech: AR(1) on daily anomalies, φ from lag-1 autocorrelation over n = 400, innovation sd 0.04 °C; e-folding time −1/ln φ; h-step forecast x·φ^h with variance σ²(1−φ^{2h})/(1−φ²), 80 % band ±1.28σ_h. Mean reversion is to the 1991–2020 climatology, which is what makes this a floor, not a prediction, during an event.
caveats: during an El Niño the anomaly does not revert to zero on this timescale: persistence underestimates the coming months on purpose
no seasonality, no forcing: a baseline only

kpis.plain: Over the last 90 days the anomaly moved +1.27 °C per month on average; 95 % interval +0.78 … +1.76.

kpis.name: trend, 30 days
kpis.plain: The last month alone: -1.57 °C per month, faster than the 90-day pace.

kpis.name: probability of rising
kpis.plain: With a flat prior, the chance that the true 90-day slope is positive is 100 % (p = 0.000 two-sided).

kpis.name: acceleration
kpis.plain: Positive: the rise is speeding up; negative: it is slowing or turning.

method.name: Linear regression with a robust (Newey–West) error
method.plain: We draw the straight line that fits the last 90 days best and ask how sure we are of its slope. Daily values are not independent (warm days come in runs), so the ordinary error would be too optimistic; the Newey–West correction widens it honestly. The “probability of rising” is the Bayesian reading of the same numbers with no prior opinion.
method.tech: OLS on daily anomalies to 1991–2020, n = 90 and 30; HAC standard error with Bartlett weights, lag 7; two-sided p from the normal approximation; P(slope > 0) = Φ(t) under a flat prior. Residual sd 1.35 °C. Acceleration = slope(last 30) − slope(days −90…−30).
caveats: a 30-day slope is noisy: read it with its interval, not alone
a trend says where the series went, not where it will go; the analogue forecast is a separate method

items.title: Regime shift in Antarctic 2 m: 2025-11-03, -1.61 °C (could be noise)

kpis.name: most likely break
kpis.plain: The day that best splits the last 400 days into “before” and “after”: mean +2.56 °C before, +0.95 °C after.

kpis.name: shift of the mean
kpis.plain: How much the average level jumped at the break.

kpis.name: chance it is noise
kpis.plain: Out of 300 random series with the same memory and spread, 159 produced a break at least this sharp. Small means the shift is real.

method.name: Change-point by binary segmentation, tested against red noise
method.plain: We try every day as a possible turning point and pick the one where the average before and after differ most. Then we ask whether a series with no real turn, only memory and noise, could show a jump this big by chance; if it rarely can, the shift is real.
method.tech: Single mean-shift change-point: max over t of |m₁−m₂|·√(t(n−t)/n)/sd, n = 400. Null: AR(1) with fitted φ = 0.95 and matched variance, 300 simulations, p = share with a larger statistic. Multiple breaks are not modelled.
caveats: one break only: a series with several turns shows the biggest
the break date is uncertain by days to weeks

items.title: Inertia of Antarctic 2 m: memory 18 days, persistence says +0.08 °C in two weeks

kpis.name: memory of the series
kpis.plain: Day-to-day persistence φ = 0.95: a departure fades to a third in about 18 days if nothing pushes it.

kpis.name: persistence forecast, +14 d
kpis.plain: If the series only had its memory, in two weeks it would sit at +0.08 °C (80 % band ±1.74).

kpis.name: persistence forecast, +30 d
kpis.plain: In a month: +0.03 °C (80 % band ±1.92).

method.name: AR(1) persistence model
method.plain: The simplest forecast is “tomorrow looks like today, a little less so each day”. We measure how strongly each day follows the previous one and let that memory fade forward. It is the baseline any real forecast must beat; the analogue forecast on the panel is the other reading.
method.tech: AR(1) on daily anomalies, φ from lag-1 autocorrelation over n = 400, innovation sd 0.50 °C; e-folding time −1/ln φ; h-step forecast x·φ^h with variance σ²(1−φ^{2h})/(1−φ²), 80 % band ±1.28σ_h. Mean reversion is to the 1991–2020 climatology, which is what makes this a floor, not a prediction, during an event.
caveats: during an El Niño the anomaly does not revert to zero on this timescale: persistence underestimates the coming months on purpose
no seasonality, no forcing: a baseline only

items.title: Years like 2026 by the January–August path: 26 in the cluster, nearest 1997, 2015, 2023

kpis.name: cluster of 2026
kpis.plain: By the shape of January–August, 2026 sits with 2006, 2009, 2012, 2014, 2017, 2018, 2023, 2025….

kpis.name: where that cluster peaks
kpis.plain: Among the complete years of the cluster, the average month and height of the peak of Niño 3.4.

kpis.name: nearest years
kpis.plain: The five years whose January–August path is closest to this one, by plain distance.

kpis.name: canonical analogues in the cluster
kpis.plain: Of the panel’s hand-picked analogues (1982, 1997, 2015, 2023), 1982, 1997, 2023 fall in the same statistical cluster.

method.name: k-means clustering of yearly trajectories
method.plain: Every year since 1950 is a short line: the monthly Niño 3.4 anomaly from January to August. We let the computer sort those lines into four families by shape, with no names attached, and see which family this year lands in and what those years did next. It is a second opinion on the hand-picked analogues.
method.tech: Features: ERSST Niño 3.4 monthly anomalies Jan–Aug (8 dims, standardised), years 1950–2026; k-means, k = 4, 10 inits, seed 0; silhouette 0.32. Nearest years by Euclidean distance in the same space. Peak month and height from complete years of the cluster.
caveats: k = 4 is a choice, not a discovery; the silhouette is modest, so cluster edges are soft
eight months of one index cannot see the subsurface, which is where events are decided

items.title: How unusual: July–August 2026 at +1.81 °C is the 100th percentile, a once-in-23-years height for a yearly peak

kpis.name: July–August level
kpis.plain: The mean of July and August 2026 in the monthly ERSST index.

kpis.name: percentile among years
kpis.plain: Higher than 100 % of all July–August values since 1950; the previous highest was 2015 at +1.42.

kpis.name: return period of this height as a yearly peak
kpis.plain: Fitting a distribution to the yearly maxima of the index, a peak of +1.81 °C or more is expected about once in 23 years — and this is only the summer value, before the usual winter peak.

method.name: Empirical percentile and a GEV return period
method.plain: Two ways to say “how rare”: the plain count of past years below this level, and a fitted curve for yearly peaks (the generalised extreme-value distribution) that turns the height into “once in N years”. The curve is the standard tool for floods and heatwaves; here it rates an El Niño peak.
method.tech: ERSST Niño 3.4 monthly anomalies, 1950–2026. Percentile: share of years with a lower Jul–Aug mean. GEV fitted by maximum likelihood (scipy) to the annual maxima of the monthly index (n = 76); return period 1/(1−F(v)). The fit treats years as independent and stationary, which warming makes only approximately true.
caveats: the summer value is compared with yearly peaks that usually come in winter: the true peak of this event is still ahead
GEV on ~75 points has wide uncertainty above the record; treat the return period as an order of magnitude

items.title: The fuel leads the surface by 6 months (r = 0.49) on the whole record since 1980

kpis.name: best lead of the fuel
kpis.plain: The warm-water volume lines up best with Niño 3.4 6 months later: r = 0.49 over 554 months, so the line accounts for about 24 % of the variation and the rest is other things. Same window as the fuel card: the whole PMEL record, 1980-01 to 2026-07.

kpis.name: what the fuel implies
kpis.plain: A straight line fitted from Niño 3.4 on the fuel 6 months earlier, then read at the latest fuel value, 3.24·10¹⁴ m³: the middle of the fit is +0.91 °C and one standard error of the fit is ±0.67, hence +0.2 to +1.6. The fuel is now at the very top of the window the line was fitted on (1980 onward), so this is the edge of what the line has ever seen and the middle of it reads low against what the surface already shows. Read the width, not the centre. This is a scale of how much the stored heat matters, not a forecast of the level.

method.name: Cross-correlation at monthly leads and a linear map
method.plain: The recharge–discharge idea says the warm water stored below the equator feeds the surface months later. We check it on our own numbers: shift the fuel series forward month by month and see where it lines up best with Niño 3.4, then use that alignment as a crude ruler.
method.tech: Pearson r between PMEL warm water volume (monthly, 1980-01…2026-07) and ERSST Niño 3.4 at leads 0–12 months; best lead 6, r = 0.49, n = 554. Linear regression of Niño 3.4(t+6) on WWV(t): slope 0.28 °C per 10¹⁴ m³, intercept +0.00.
caveats: the lead is measured on four decades of monthly data, the same ruler as the fuel card; the literature puts it at 6–9 months
the fit mixes the charge and discharge phases; during an event the relation flattens

items.title: Bayesian peak: median +3.09 °C, 95 % to top 1997, 89 % to top 2015

kpis.name: implied winter peak
kpis.plain: Scaling this year’s July–August level (+1.81) by how much past events grew from summer to their peak: median +3.09 °C, 80 % band +2.16 … +4.03, from 12 past events.

kpis.name: chance to top 1997
kpis.plain: The 1997–98 peak in this index was +1.85 °C.

kpis.name: chance to top 2015
kpis.plain: The 2015–16 peak was +2.21 °C.

kpis.name: chance to top 2023
kpis.plain: The 2023–24 peak was +1.86 °C.

method.name: Empirical-Bayes ensemble of implied peaks
method.plain: Every past event that was already under way by August grew from its summer level to its winter peak by some factor. We apply each of those factors to this summer, get a spread of possible peaks, and read off the odds of beating the famous years. The spread is treated with a Student-t predictive distribution, which is the Bayesian answer when the mean and the scatter are both unknown.
method.tech: ERSST Niño 3.4 monthly; events = years with Jul–Aug mean ≥ 0.5 °C (n = 12); ratio = max(Sep–Dec)/mean(Jul–Aug); implied = ratio × Jul–Aug 2026; flat prior on (μ, σ²) → Student-t predictive with df = n−1, scale s√(1+1/n); P(peak > record) from its tail. Members: 1957, 1965, 1972, 1987, 1991, 1997, 2002, 2004, 2009, 2015, 2019, 2023.
caveats: the peak is taken within September–December of the same year; a January peak is missed for some events
the ensemble treats all past events as exchangeable; the subsurface charge of this year (at its record) is not used, so the odds may be conservative

items.title: Teleconnection strength on our boxes, 45 summers: strongest air link Peru coast (r +0.53); rain links hold in 4 boxes

kpis.name: strongest air link
kpis.plain: July–August air over Peru coast moves +0.74 °C per 1 °C of Niño 3.4 (p = 0.000, 45 years).

kpis.name: rain links that hold
kpis.plain: Peru coast: drier with El Niño, -4 mm per °C, r -0.35; Java: drier with El Niño, -84 mm per °C, r -0.56; East Africa: drier with El Niño, -30 mm per °C, r -0.33; Northern India: drier with El Niño, -62 mm per °C, r -0.33

kpis.name: this summer against the link
kpis.unit: boxes warmer than El Niño alone predicts
kpis.plain: Kuwait and the northern Gulf +1.4 °C; Central Europe +0.8 °C; Peru coast +1.6 °C; Java +0.9 °C; East Africa +0.8 °C; Northern India -0.2 °C

method.name: Cross-year linear regression of the box on Niño 3.4
method.plain: For each of our six land boxes we take the same July–August window in every year since 1981: the mean air temperature and the rain sum. We plot them against the Niño 3.4 of that summer and fit a line. The slope is how much a degree of El Niño usually buys that region; the correlation says how reliable the link is; this year is then compared with what the line predicts from Niño 3.4 alone.
method.tech: ERA5 box means and box precipitation sums (spectral/*-box.json, *-precip.json), Jul 1–Aug 31 each year 1981–2025 (≥ 40 days), against ERSST Niño 3.4 Jul–Aug mean; OLS slope, Pearson r, two-sided p (normal approximation); the current year is held out and reported as residual from the fitted line. Rows in `table`.
caveats: July–August is the wrong season for many teleconnections (India monsoon, Peru winter): a weak link here does not mean no link
45 points, one predictor: warming trend is not removed and can masquerade as an El Niño effect in the air regressions

items.title: Where the nearest years went from this day: median +3.15 °C in 90 days (range +2.34 … +3.94)

kpis.name: nearest years by the January–August path
kpis.plain: Their daily Niño 3.4 from this calendar day on, shifted so that each starts at today’s value.

kpis.name: +30 days
kpis.plain: Median of the 5 paths; range +2.47 … +3.16.

kpis.name: +60 days
kpis.plain: Median of the 5 paths; range +2.01 … +3.65.

kpis.name: +90 days
kpis.plain: Median of the 5 paths; range +2.34 … +3.94. Today: +2.65.

method.name: Analogue ensemble, nearest years, shifted to today
method.plain: We take the five years whose January–August looked most like this one, follow what their Niño 3.4 did over the next three months from this calendar day, and start every path from today’s value so that only the shape matters. The median is the central expectation, the range is the honest spread.
method.tech: Nearest years by Euclidean distance in standardised ERSST Jan–Aug space (same as the clusters item); daily OISST anomalies (climatereanalyzer) from day-of-year 242, horizons 0–90 days in 15-day steps; each path offset by (today − that year’s value on the same day). Median and min–max across paths.
caveats: five paths: the range is wide by construction and says nothing about probabilities beyond it
shifting to today removes the level difference but keeps each year’s own weather; the record height of this year has no analogue

items.title: Food prices follow Niño 3.4 with a lag of 12 months (r = 0.20, 1991–2025); most sensitive: Oils

kpis.name: food index follows Niño 3.4 by
kpis.plain: Best correlation between the year-on-year change of the FAO index and Niño 3.4 12 months earlier: r = 0.20 over 420 months since 1991; +3.9 points of yearly change per 1 °C.

kpis.name: most sensitive group
kpis.plain: Oils: lag 12 mo, r 0.33, +12.4 pt/°C; Dairy: lag 12 mo, r 0.20, +6.4 pt/°C; Cereals: lag 12 mo, r 0.11, +2.9 pt/°C; Sugar: lag 0 mo, r 0.05, +2.1 pt/°C; Meat: lag 12 mo, r -0.03, -0.4 pt/°C

kpis.name: least sensitive group
kpis.plain: A weak or negative correlation means that group has followed other drivers (energy, trade, disease) more than El Niño.

method.name: Cross-correlation of year-on-year price change with Niño 3.4 at monthly lags, plus a linear slope
method.plain: Prices trend upward for many reasons, so we look at their yearly change instead of the level, and ask how far behind the ocean it lags: we shift Niño 3.4 back month by month and find the shift where the two lines agree best, for the whole index and for each food group. The slope says how many points of yearly change one degree of Niño 3.4 has been worth.
method.tech: FAO Food Price Index and five groups (2014–2016 = 100), year-on-year % change, 1990-01…2025-12 (2026 held out); ERSST Niño 3.4 monthly anomaly at lags 0–12; Pearson r at each lag, best reported; OLS slope of yoy on Niño 3.4 at the best lag. No detrending beyond the yoy transform; no control for oil, dollar or trade shocks.
caveats: correlations of 0.2–0.4 over 400 months are real but small: El Niño is one driver among several
the 2007–08 and 2022 spikes were not El Niño; they sit in the sample and dilute the link

items.title: Warm crest at 100 m: at 131°W, drifting +10.8° per month (+0.46 m/s)

kpis.name: warm crest now
kpis.plain: Centre of the warm anomaly at 100 m along the equator in 2026-07; in 2025-12 it was at 148°E.

kpis.name: eastward drift
kpis.plain: Fitted over the last 8 months: +0.46 m/s. A free Kelvin wave crosses at 2–3 m/s; a slow drift means the warm pool is being displaced, not a single wave passing.

kpis.name: warm area at 100 m
kpis.plain: Share of the equatorial section warmer than +0.5 °C at 100 m in the latest month.

method.name: Centre of mass of the warm anomaly and its drift by regression
method.plain: On the Hovmöller picture time runs down and longitude across. For each month we find where the warm water below the surface is centred, then fit a line through those centres over the last months: its slope is how fast the warmth is moving east, in degrees per month, converted to metres per second at the equator.
method.tech: GODAS anomaly at 100 m along the equator, monthly; crest = anomaly-weighted mean longitude of positive anomalies (months with max ≥ 0.5 °C); OLS of crest on month index over the last 8 months; 1° ≈ 111 km. Kelvin-wave speed for reference: 2–3 m/s.
caveats: monthly steps cannot resolve a single Kelvin wave (weeks); this measures the slow migration of the warm pool
the centre of mass moves also when the west cools, not only when the east warms

items.title: Land boxes by air and rain: 2 groups; rain follows the analogue years in 3 of 5

kpis.name: regional weather groups
kpis.plain: hot-dry: Kuwait and the northern Gulf, Java, East Africa; hot: Central Europe, Peru coast, Northern India

kpis.name: rain like the analogue years
kpis.plain: Same sign as the mean of 1982/1997/2015/2023 in: Java, East Africa, Northern India. Opposite: Kuwait and the northern Gulf, Peru coast.

kpis.name: most unusual air
kpis.plain: 30-day air anomaly +3.3 °C, +4.3 standard deviations from this window in 1981–2025.

method.name: Quadrant classification against normal and against analogue years
method.plain: Each of our six land boxes is placed by two numbers: how warm the air was over the last 30 days against normal, and how much rain fell against normal. That gives simple families (hot and dry, hot and wet…). Then we ask whether the rain sign this year matches what the same 30 days did in the four strongest past events — the teleconnection check on our own boxes.
method.tech: ERA5 box means (regions_daily.py) and box precipitation sums (precip.py): air anomaly and z-score of the last 30 days against the same window 1981–2025; rain as % of the 1991–2020 normal; thresholds hot > +0.5 °C, dry < 80 %, wet > 120 %; analogue rain = mean of the four events’ same-window sums as % of normal.
caveats: six boxes are a sample, not the world; thresholds are conventions
dry-season boxes (the Gulf in summer) have tiny normals: percentages there mean little

items.title: Storms and the sea this summer: Niño 1+2 follows the convection by 18 days (r = 0.40, 74 days)
items.series: radiance conv_frac nino34_A vs OISST boxes

kpis.name: convection → Niño 1+2
kpis.plain: Niño 1+2 off Peru follows the convection by 18 days (r = 0.40, 74 days)

kpis.name: convection → Niño 3.4
kpis.plain: Niño 3.4 surface leads the convection by 8 days (r = 0.39, 74 days)

method.name: Cross-correlation at daily lags
method.plain: We slide the daily share of deep storm clouds over Niño 3.4 (from the satellite) against the daily sea-surface anomalies of Niño 1+2 and Niño 3.4 and look for the shift in days where they agree best. A positive shift means the sea follows the storms; negative, the storms follow the sea.
method.tech: Pearson r between CrIS conv_frac (day node) and OISST box anomalies over common days of the 2026 window, lags ±20 days, maximum reported; series are short (~2 months) and autocorrelated, so r is optimistic and the lag is uncertain by several days.
caveats: two months of daily data: exploratory, not a mechanism
both series carry the seasonal rise; part of the correlation is the common trend

items.title: Twenty years of the same window: 2026 convection over Niño 3.4 is rank 1 of 22, ×1.7 the super El Niño of 2015

kpis.name: Niño 3.4, day: rank of 2026
kpis.plain: Deep-convection share 9.2 % ± 0.6; the 2003–2021 median is 0.6 %; robust z = 19 (median absolute deviation scale).

kpis.name: against 2015 on two instruments
kpis.plain: Ratios of the 2026 window mean to the 2015 window mean brought to the NOAA-21 scale; the difference is 4.8, 4.6 standard errors, so it is not noise.

kpis.name: trend 2003–2021 before this event
kpis.plain: Linear trend of the yearly window means over the calibrated history; small against the jump of 2026, so the record is the event, not a drift of the record.

kpis.name: warm pool, day: rank of 2026
kpis.plain: The west has the least deep cloud of the record: 7.5 % against a median of 12.0 %; the east–west contrast has never been this inverted in the record.

method.name: Ranks, robust z and ratios on a calibrated multi-instrument record
method.plain: Four instruments over twenty years do not read exactly alike, so the collector first measures each instrument’s offset against NOAA-21 on days they overlapped, then shifts every year onto one scale. On that record we rank this year, compare it with the median of 2003–2021 using a scale that ignores outliers, and test the gap to 2015 against the standard errors of both years.
method.tech: epochs block of radiance.json: adjusted yearly window means with SE; best instrument per year (CrIS chain first, AIRS ≤ 2021); rank among all years; robust z = (x − median)/(1.4826·MAD) over 2003–2021; ratio and (x₂₀₂₆ − x₂₀₁₅)/√(se₁² + se₂²) per instrument; OLS trend over 2003–2021.
caveats: offsets are measured on a few hundred overlapping days: a residual bias of order the SE cannot be excluded
AIRS years after 2021 are excluded because its overpass drifted into the afternoon cloud maximum

items.title: Momentum: 13 of 21 key indicators moved toward a stronger event at their last change (62 %)

kpis.name: indicators moving toward a stronger event
kpis.plain: Niño 3.4, weekly anomaly, Niño 3.4, daily anomaly, Niño 3.4, mean of 30 days, Niño 3.4, our box, daily NRT, ONI, official, World ocean, 60°S–60°N, anomaly, Westerly anomaly, 130°E–180°, 7-day, Model peak, combined, Models below reality, Risk index…

kpis.name: moving the other way
kpis.plain: Niño 1+2, weekly anomaly, Niño 1+2, our box, daily NRT, Land + ocean, 2 m, anomaly, Mean over the live models, Models that broke, Southern Oscillation Index, Convection at the date line, Persian Gulf SST, daily

kpis.name: chance of this lopsidedness by coin-flip
kpis.plain: If each indicator moved up or down at random, a split of 13:8 or more lopsided would happen 19.2 % of the time.

kpis.name: unchanged since the previous reading
kpis.plain: Trade wind, western Pacific, Atmospheric signs in place, MJO amplitude (OMI)

method.name: Sign count over the value journal with a binomial test
method.plain: Every indicator in the journal has a direction that means “the event is getting stronger” — warmer water, more fuel, weaker trades, more models below reality. We take each indicator’s last change and count how many went that way. A coin-flip test says how surprising the split is. It is a crude but honest pulse: one number for the whole board.
method.tech: 24 journal metrics with ≥ 2 entries and a defined sign (SOI and OLR count reversed; MJO amplitude undirected); direction of the last change; one-sided binomial test of ups against 0.5. Changes are of unequal age (weekly, daily, monthly series), so this is a snapshot of the latest moves, not a rate.
caveats: indicators are not independent: Niño 3.4 weekly, daily and box are the same water
a change of one tick counts like a big one; magnitude is on the KPI strip

items.title: System stability: autocorrelation rising, variance rising, series moving together more than usual
items.series: sst_nino34 daily + all daily series + spectral

kpis.name: autocorrelation trend
kpis.plain: Kendall trend of the lag-1 autocorrelation of detrended Niño 3.4 in a 90-day sliding window over the last 400 days: now 0.97, median 0.93. Rising memory is the classic sign of a system losing its grip — or, during an event, of a system already in the new state.

kpis.name: variance trend
kpis.plain: Kendall trend of the 90-day variance of the detrended series: now 0.027, median 0.008 °C². Growing swings are the second classic sign.

kpis.name: series moving together
kpis.plain: Mean absolute correlation of the 8 daily series (ocean, world air, hemispheres, tropics, poles) over the last 120 days, against the same window of the previous five years. Higher means the whole system is being driven by one thing.

kpis.name: spectral lines at 99 %
kpis.plain: Lines at 1–7 days across all daily series (Dynamics · Spectral watch): the owner’s hypothesis of a comb before a spontaneous transition.

kpis.name: flags raised
kpis.plain: autocorrelation rising, variance rising, series moving together more than usual

method.name: Early-warning indicators of a critical transition (Scheffer), plus coherence
method.plain: Before a system tips into a new state it usually gets slower to recover and swings wider: the memory of the series (autocorrelation) and its variance both climb. We compute both in a sliding window on the daily Niño 3.4, detrended so the event’s own rise does not fake the signal, and test whether they trend up. We add whether the world’s daily series have started moving together more than they used to, and the spectral watch. Each raised flag lifts the level. This is a watch, not a verdict: during a strong event the indicators also rise simply because the state has changed.
method.tech: Residuals of Niño 3.4 daily anomalies after a 30-day running mean; 90-day sliding windows, step 5, over 400 days; lag-1 AC and variance per window; Kendall τ against time (flag τ > 0.3; extra level if both τ > 0.5). Coherence: mean |r| of the 8 daily series over 120 days vs the median of the same window in the previous five years (flag if > 1.25×). Spectral: lines at 99 % vs expected by chance (flag if > 2×). Level = 1 + flags (+1), capped at 5.
caveats: early-warning indicators are designed for a system approaching a tipping point; an El Niño already under way raises them for a different reason
ocean currents are not in this: OSCAR and altimetry need registration (pending), so the circulation itself is watched only through the Walker contrast on the satellite

flags: series moving together more than usual

items.title: Who moves with whom: 1 groups among 8 daily series; the tropical air follows Niño 3.4 with a lag of about 26 days (r = 0.92)

kpis.name: groups moving together
kpis.plain: Niño 3.4 (OISST) + world ocean (OISST) + land+ocean 2 m (ERA5) + northern hemisphere 2 m + southern hemisphere 2 m + tropics 2 m + Arctic 2 m + Antarctic 2 m

kpis.name: closest pair
kpis.plain: Niño 3.4 (OISST) and world ocean (OISST) rise and fall together over the last 110 days.

kpis.name: most independent pair
kpis.plain: Arctic 2 m and Antarctic 2 m hardly share day-to-day moves.

kpis.name: ocean → tropical air lag
kpis.plain: the tropical air follows Niño 3.4 with a lag of about 26 days (r = 0.92)

method.name: Correlation matrix, hierarchical clustering and cross-correlation lag
method.plain: We line up the daily anomalies of the ocean and of the air over the world, the hemispheres, the tropics and the poles over the same days and see which pairs breathe together. Then we group them by similarity and ask whether the tropical air trails the Pacific surface by some days.
method.tech: Pearson correlations of daily anomalies over 110 common days; average-linkage hierarchical clustering on 1−r, cut at 0.6; lag by maximising the cross-correlation of Niño 3.4 against tropics 2 m over the last 400 days, ±45 days.
caveats: correlation over 120 days is dominated by the seasonal march and weather, not by El Niño alone
a lag of days is not a mechanism; it says which series turns first

items.title: Spectral watch: 0 lines at 99 % against 1.7 expected by chance

kpis.name: lines at 99 % now
kpis.plain: Across all daily series and periods 1–7 days, 0 spectral lines pass the 99 % level; by chance alone about 1.7 would.

kpis.name: verdict of the watch
kpis.value: 24 daily series scanned for a line at 2–7 days over the last
kpis.plain: 24 daily series scanned for a line at 2–7 days over the last 30 days: no signal; 0 line(s) at 99 % against 1.7 expected by chance.

method.name: Periodogram against a red-noise background (already on the panel)
method.plain: Each daily series is tested for a regular beat of one to seven days in a sliding 30-day window; a line counts only if it stands far above what a noisy series with memory would show. The count of such lines against the number expected by chance is the watch.
